title: ERP / Systems Consolidation
summary: Consolidating fragmented finance and operating systems into one scalable control layer.
definition: ERP / Systems Consolidation is the process of moving a portfolio company or acquisition platform from fragmented systems to a standardized operating and reporting backbone.
whyItMatters: PE cares because fragmented systems delay reporting, hide integration risk, weaken KPI visibility, and reduce exit readiness.
commonProblems: Add-ons operate on separate finance, inventory, HR, or CRM systems.
Reporting depends on spreadsheets and manual reconciliations.
Management cannot produce consistent site, customer, SKU, or segment profitability.
diagnosticQuestions: Which systems are the source of truth for finance, operations, customers, inventory, and people?
What reporting or integration pain is caused by fragmentation?
Which consolidation path creates value without overwhelming the organization?
dataNeeded: Chart of accounts, master data, and reporting definitions
Process maps for quote-to-cash, procure-to-pay, record-to-report, and order-to-fulfillment
Integration, license, implementation, and support cost data
process: Map current systems, data flows, pain points, and reporting gaps.
Define target architecture and migration priorities.
Standardize chart of accounts, master data, and process ownership.
Execute phased migration with controls, testing, and change management.
Retire legacy systems and embed reporting governance.
ebitdaLogic: Systems consolidation improves EBITDA and exit value by reducing manual work, enabling integration synergies, improving operating visibility, and creating buyer confidence in scalability.
caseExample: A buy-and-build platform migrates five acquired entities onto one ERP, standardizes the chart of accounts, and finally produces branch-level profitability within the monthly close.
hundredDayPlan: Days 1-30: inventory systems, data flows, reporting gaps, and integration pain.
Days 31-60: define target architecture, migration waves, governance, and resourcing.
Days 61-100: launch first standardization wave, clean master data, and create executive migration dashboard.
commonMistakes: Treating ERP consolidation as IT plumbing instead of operating model redesign.
Migrating bad data and broken processes into a newer system.
Launching a big-bang implementation without enough management bandwidth.

articleSections.title: Baseline Applications, Processes, Data, and Control Risk
body: Inventory the estate by legal entity, site, process, interface, contract, user, and data owner. The CIO should map ERP, CRM, warehouse, payroll, billing, planning, and reporting systems, while process owners identify the spreadsheets and manual workarounds that actually run the business. Record license and support cost, version, customization, integration method, security status, close dependency, and replacement constraint. A nominal system list misses the real risk when an unsupported database, one employee's macro, or a nightly flat-file transfer controls revenue recognition or customer shipment.

Baseline critical processes before selecting software. Walk quote-to-cash, procure-to-pay, plan-to-produce, inventory-to-fulfillment, record-to-report, and hire-to-retire across representative sites. Measure touch time, queue time, error and rework, approval steps, reconciliations, close days, and control evidence. Separate process inconsistency from system limitation: moving twelve different customer-master rules into a modern ERP preserves twelve bad processes at a higher cost. Finance, operations, and commercial leaders must sign the current-state facts rather than delegating transformation entirely to IT.

Quantify the cost and risk case with a reconciled baseline. One $300 million roll-up operated five ledgers, three warehouse systems, and 146 recurring spreadsheet reconciliations. It spent $4.8 million annually on licenses, hosting, contractors, and support, plus roughly $2.1 million of internal labor on duplicate administration and reconciliation. The monthly close took fifteen business days, inventory adjustments averaged $900,000 per quarter, and add-on reporting required ten weeks. Those measures established the value pool and the operational constraints that the target design had to improve.
articleSections.callout: Consolidation starts with process and control facts; software is the mechanism, not the operating model.

articleSections.title: Design the Target Architecture and Select to Fit
body: Define principles before products: one chart of accounts, authoritative customer and item masters, standard APIs, role-based access, a governed analytics layer, and local variation only where regulation or operating economics require it. Decide which capabilities belong in the ERP and which remain specialized applications. A warehouse execution tool or industry billing engine may be strategically necessary; forcing every function into one suite can create expensive customization. The target architecture should show systems of record, ownership, integration, data latency, security zones, and the repeatable pattern for future acquisitions.

Translate processes into weighted requirements and scripted demonstrations. Vendors should execute company scenarios such as a partial shipment with rebate accrual, intercompany transfer, lot recall, milestone invoice, and add-on entity close using representative data. Score functional fit, implementation capacity, total cost, extensibility, controls, reporting, support, and integration—not polished generic demos. Architecture and finance jointly own the recommendation; process leaders approve fit; procurement validates commercials; the board approves only after independent challenge of customizations, implementation assumptions, and vendor references.

Use stage gates to prevent selection momentum from overriding evidence. No vendor enters final negotiation until target processes and data ownership are approved. No contract is signed without a five-year total-cost model, implementation statement of work, named internal resources, exit rights, and a tested implementation plan. A solution that requires extensive customization should lose unless the deviation creates measurable competitive advantage. Otherwise each customization becomes upgrade friction, control complexity, and diligence debt that follows the platform into the next transaction.

articleSections.title: Migrate in Controlled Waves and Protect the Cutover
body: Sequence waves around business risk and organizational capacity. Establish the global template and master-data model, pilot a representative but manageable entity, correct defects, then roll by site or business unit. Each wave owns data cleansing, mapping, mock conversions, interface testing, role design, training, and local cutover. Avoid launching during peak season, year-end close, or a major integration unless survival requires it. The program manager maintains one dependency plan, while local leaders remain accountable for process readiness instead of treating deployment as an IT handoff.

Migration controls should reconcile completeness and accuracy from source to target. Compare record counts, control totals, open orders, receivables, payables, inventory quantity and value, fixed assets, and trial balances; sample customer and item attributes; retain lineage for audit. Require user acceptance against end-to-end scenarios, segregation-of-duties review, disaster recovery, interface monitoring, and signed process-owner acceptance. A data conversion is not successful merely because the file loaded; it succeeds when transactions post correctly, controls operate, and the old system can be retired without losing evidence.

Cutover uses explicit go/no-go criteria and a rollback plan. Gates include critical-defect closure, reconciled mock conversions, trained super-users, stable integrations, support coverage, backup completion, and business-continuity workarounds. During hypercare, a command center triages severity-one order, billing, inventory, payroll, and close defects with named owners and response times. Track service levels and working capital daily so the team does not declare technical success while shipments stall or invoices age. Exit hypercare only after two stable transaction cycles and a clean close.

articleSections.title: Drive Adoption Through Governance and Process Ownership
body: Adoption is measured in compliant transactions, not training attendance. Role-based instruction should use real workflows, with proficiency checks for buyers, planners, sales operations, warehouse staff, accountants, and approvers. A network of site super-users resolves questions and feeds defects to the central team. Managers review exception reports for off-system purchases, manual journal entries, duplicate masters, late approvals, and spreadsheet shadow systems. If users can bypass the new design without consequence, the company will pay for both old and new operating models.

Governance must distinguish defects, enhancements, and resistance to standardization. A weekly design authority chaired by the CIO and CFO approves changes based on control, economic value, and template impact; process owners decide operating policy; the systems integrator provides options but cannot own the decision. Release windows, documentation, testing, and access approval continue after go-live. The board receives monthly status on milestones, cost, risks, adoption, service continuity, and benefits, with escalation for budget variance, critical control failures, or wave slippage.

Change failure often begins with unclear consequences. Explain which roles and tasks will change, provide transition support, and make decisions early about duplicate jobs rather than allowing rumors to fill the gap. Tie executive objectives to process adoption and benefit capture, not just on-time deployment. Protect high-performing local practices when they create customer value, but require evidence before deviating from the template. This balance prevents two extremes: headquarters imposing an unusable model and local teams preserving every legacy preference under the label of uniqueness.

articleSections.title: Validate Benefits and Prove a Scalable Exit Platform
body: Finance should freeze the pre-program baseline and maintain a benefit ledger by source: retired license and support cost, contractor reduction, eliminated duplicate roles, close labor, inventory accuracy, billing speed, working-capital release, and integration capacity. Benefits count only after contracts terminate, payroll changes occur, cycle time improves, or cash is realized; avoid adding a working-capital release to recurring EBITDA. Charge implementation cost, stranded cost, and temporary productivity loss transparently so the investment committee sees net economics rather than a vendor business case.

In the $300 million roll-up, the program retired four ledgers and two warehouse platforms. Annual third-party run-rate cost fell from $4.8 million to $3.1 million, duplicate administrative labor fell $1.2 million, and reduced reconciliation effort freed $700,000, for $3.6 million of gross recurring benefit. After $600,000 of added central data and support roles, validated net run-rate benefit was $3.0 million. A $12 million implementation therefore implied a four-year simple payback before counting a five-day faster close, a $4 million inventory reduction, or faster add-on onboarding.

Exit proof should show more than a go-live date. Package the target architecture, system-retirement evidence, standardized controls, master-data governance, close and service trends, benefit ledger, security posture, and the playbook for onboarding the next acquisition. Demonstrate that a new entity can map its chart, customers, products, roles, and interfaces into the template within a predictable schedule and cost. Buyers underwrite a premium when the platform can add volume and acquisitions without recreating back-office complexity; unresolved customizations, shadow systems, or unsupported interfaces undermine that claim.
